# ONNX Dialect (selected sections)

The ONNX dialect (`src/Dialect/ONNX/`) is the primary representation of the neural network graph within onnx-mlir. It mirrors the ONNX operator set, adds shape inference interfaces, and serves as the input to all graph-level transformations.

## `--recompose-onnx`

Fuses sequences of ops back into more efficient compound ops when beneficial. Implemented as hand-written `mlir::OpRewritePattern` C++ classes in `Recompose.cpp` (e.g. `RecomposeLayerNormFromMulPattern`, `RecomposeGeluFromMulPattern`, `CombineParallelConv2DPattern`) — not TableGen DRR rules; `Recompose.cpp` even has the DRR include commented out.

One pattern in this set is opt-in rather than always registered: `RecomposeAttentionFromMatMulPattern` is inserted by `getRecomposeONNXToONNXPatterns()` only when `--enable-attention-op-construct` is passed (default `false`, see [compiler.md](compiler.md)). It matches a hand-written scaled-dot-product-attention subgraph rooted at the second `MatMul` — `MatMul(Q, Transpose(K))` (the transpose swapping only the last two dims), optionally scaled by a `Div`/`Mul` against a scalar dense constant, optionally followed by `Add(attn_mask)`, then `Softmax` over the last axis, then `MatMul(·, V)` — and rewrites the whole chain to a single `onnx.Attention` built through `OnnxBuilder::attention()`, folding the scaling into the op's `scale` attribute (`1/divisor` for the `Div` form, the constant itself for the `Mul` form; `1.0` when unscaled). Every intermediate value must have exactly one use, and Q/K/V must be rank 3 or 4 with no leading "batch-like" axis statically known to differ, because `ONNXAttentionOpShapeHelper` derives `batch_size` (and 4-D `q_num_heads`) from Q alone and won't replicate broadcasting the decomposed MatMuls would have tolerated. Dynamic dimensions are currently *assumed* to agree rather than proven: `DimAnalysis` is a whole-module analysis and isn't available inside Recompose, which sees one `func::FuncOp` at a time before shape inference has run — a limitation recorded as a `TODO` in the pattern itself.[^2]

### `SplitMatMulBySlicePattern`

Registered by default (opt-out via `--disable-split-matmul-by-slice`, an `OnnxMlirCommonOptions` flag, default `false`). It targets the gated-MLP (SwiGLU/GeGLU) idiom where the gate and up projections are one `MatMul` followed by `Slice`s of its output: when `MatMul(X, W)` has a dense-constant `W` and either **every** user is a `Slice` of the result along the last axis with step 1 and constant bounds, or its single user is a `Split` along the last axis, each `Slice` (or used `Split` output) is replaced by `MatMul(X, Slice(W, start, end))`. A `Split` is treated as one `Slice` per output, each starting where the previous one ends, with the output's static width; unused `Split` outputs are dropped. Constant propagation later folds the `Slice` of `W`. Guards: `W` must be static with rank ≥ 2; each slice must be at least `minSliceWidth = 256` wide (bounds the cost of re-reading `X` per new MatMul, and on NNPA the padding of each MatMul's last dim to 64); the slice widths must sum to at most the full output width (so no MatMul work is added); and `W` must have no other user (so it is replaced by its slices rather than kept alongside them).[^6]

### `UnbindSlicesToSplitPattern` and `PullSqueezeTransposeThroughSplitPattern`

Registered by default as a pair (opt-out via `--disable-unbind-to-split`, an `OnnxMlirCommonOptions` flag, default `false`). `UnbindSlicesToSplitPattern` matches PyTorch's `unbind` idiom: N unit-width, step-1 `Slice`s that tile a static axis of size N, each followed by a `Squeeze` of that axis, become one `Split` into N unit slices (the `Squeeze`s stay). It matches only this idiom, not every set of `Slice`s tiling an axis, so that `Slice`s of a `MatMul` output are left to `SplitMatMulBySlicePattern`. `PullSqueezeTransposeThroughSplitPattern` then hoists a `Transpose` common to all the squeezed `Split` results above the `Split` (inserting the split axis into `perm`), giving the `Reshape → Transpose → Split → Squeeze` layout that NNPA's unstick-split-heads fusion recognizes.[^15]

## `ONNXFusedOp` (internal fusion container)

`onnx.Fused` (`ONNXFusedOp`, `src/Dialect/ONNX/AdditionalONNXOps.td`, impl in `ONNXOps/Additional/FusedOp.cpp`) is a distinct mechanism from `--recompose-onnx`: an `IsolatedFromAbove` region holding a chain of matched ops, tagged with a `kind` attribute, meant to be lowered/codegen'd jointly as one unit rather than recomposed into another standard ONNX op. It's backed by a generic helper framework (`src/Dialect/ONNX/Transforms/FusionOpHelper.{hpp,cpp}`, `FusionOpBasePattern.hpp`) and consumed by both `ONNXToKrnl` and the NNPA accelerator path (see [stack/accelerators.md](../../../../.agents/skills/nnpa-internals/references/accelerators.md#op-fusion-before-lowering)).

### `--fusion-op-transform` — the CPU-side formation pass

Fused ops are formed by exactly one pass per build configuration, and which one depends on whether an accelerator is targeted:

- **CPU**: `--fusion-op-transform` (`FusionOpTransformPass`, `FusionOpTransform.cpp`, declared in `Transforms/Passes.td` as a `ModuleOp` pass) registers the non-accelerator-specific kinds via `populateONNXFusionOpPatterns()` and runs them greedily over the module, building a fresh `DimAnalysis` first since the kind helpers need dimension-equality answers to decide whether a chain is safe to fuse.
- **NNPA (or any accelerator)**: this pass is not scheduled at all. NNPA's own `FusionOpStickUnstick` calls the same `populateONNXFusionOpPatterns()` alongside its `zhigh.*` kinds, so the general kinds still get formed — just in the accelerator's own, later fusion pass. `CompilerPasses.cpp` enforces the either/or with a `targetCPU` gate.

The pass is scheduled deliberately late in `addONNXToMLIRPasses()` — after `scrub-disposable`, immediately before `set-onnx-node-name` and instrumentation — so earlier optimizations can't disturb a fused op once it exists. `--disable-fused-op` turns it off, and is checked twice: once at pipeline-construction time and again inside `runOnOperation()` (the latter is what would apply to a direct `onnx-mlir-opt --fusion-op-transform` invocation, where the flag is unsettable anyway since it belongs to the `onnx-mlir`-only category).

The CPU-side kinds live in `ONNXFusionOpHelper.{hpp,cpp}` — the counterpart of NNPA's `ZHighFusionOpHelper.{hpp,cpp}` — and there is one such kind:

- **`simd-split-op-gather`** (`SplitOpGatherFusionHelper`): the RoPE "rotate_half" idiom. An `onnx.Concat` of exactly two inputs, splitting on the innermost axis, where each input traces back through an optional single elementwise op to an `onnx.Slice` of a shared source tensor — the two slices dense (`step=1`), contiguous, and together covering the whole split axis. Restrictions in this first version: the split axis must be the innermost dimension, each slice's `axes` operand must name exactly that axis, the split point and the source's split-axis extent must both be compile-time literals, and a per-half op's extra operand must match that half's shape exactly (no broadcasting) and must not be the other half's slice. Every intermediate value must have exactly one use. The helper lays its chain-op list out in a fixed low-half-first order — `[sliceLow, opLow?, sliceHigh, opHigh?, concatOp]` — regardless of Concat's actual operand order, which is what lets `verify()` re-check the chain positionally despite two independently optional ops; consequently the ops as cloned into the fused body print low-then-high even when the source IR had them reversed. Its Krnl lowering is described in [interfaces/onnx-to-krnl.md](onnx-to-krnl.md).[^3]

Contract points of the shared `FusionOpKindHelper` framework (used by both the CPU kind above and NNPA's `zhigh.*` kinds):

- **Legality is decided only in `detectIfBeneficial()`**, which always receives a non-null `DimAnalysis` (asserted in `FusedPatternForOpKind::matchAndRewrite`) and must use it to prove every dynamic-dim equality the lowering relies on. `verify()` runs at lowering time without a `DimAnalysis`; it only re-checks that the body still has the structure and parameter values detection recorded, and may accept `?` vs `?`. A hand-written `onnx.Fused` op carries no such proof and must itself satisfy the dynamic-dim equalities.
- **Pattern benefit is `FusionT::kMaxOpCount`**, a per-kind compile-time constant (the longest chain the kind can match; `5` for `simd-split-op-gather`). It only ranks kinds anchored on the *same* op type; precedence between kinds anchored on different op types has to come from running the longer-chain kind in an earlier greedy phase.
- **Chains may be DAGs and chain ops may have several results** (e.g. `onnx.Split`): `ops` is in block order, every yielded result is redirected to its `onnx.Fused` output, and non-yielded results must already be dead.
- **Opt-in hook `absorbShapeConcatOfDims()`** (default `false`): when true, a small i64 shape `Concat` built only from constants and `onnx.Dim` results is cloned into the body (its `Dim` results become inputs) instead of becoming an input itself — for a `Concat` defined too late in the block to be a fused-op operand.[^7]
